# Feedback

the current checkout. Within this feedback cycle, this coordinator is the only
participant allowed to modify the working tree. Read
`../review/references/analysis-only.md`, `references/github.md`, and

## 1. Establish the current branch

2. Record the branch, `git rev-parse HEAD`, and `git status --short` before remote intake. Treat existing changes as user-owned unless the user identifies them otherwise.
3. Parse optional PR and trail selectors without checking out a branch or creating a worktree. Give each selector to its provider reference for repository and branch validation.
4. Stop without remote processing when an explicit selector does not match the current repository or checked-out branch. State the selector, current branch, and mismatch. Never switch branches.

## 2. Start review intake

1. Treat the recorded local `HEAD` as the candidate commit. When the working
   tree is clean, run the local analysis-only review reference against that
   commit in the same orchestration phase as GitHub discovery/reviewer intake
   and Entire discovery/watcher setup. Keep every source independent. If the
   tree is dirty, mark local analysis unavailable and continue remote intake.
2. Use only each provider's documented retry. After a failed retry of
   provider-wide discovery or core reads, retain the exact failure, mark that
   provider unavailable, and continue other sources. A local-analysis failure
   likewise does not block GitHub or Entire.
3. After initial intake, compare the candidate with the PR's `headRefOid`. On
   mismatch, discard local-analysis results, report all available read-only
   state, stop the Entire watcher, and exit before requests, edits, replies,
   status changes, commits, or pushes.
4. A missing PR or trail makes only that provider unavailable. Stop only for an

6. Request `Stale` or `Missing` Bugbot and Copilot reviews together. Do not
   duplicate a `Current` or `In flight` reviewer. A reviewer-specific failure
   marks only that reviewer unavailable.
7. Run local analysis only for the starting candidate. After this coordinator
   pushes its own fixes, focused verification covers those fixes while remote
   reviewers are refreshed against the new head.

## 3. Collect the candidate review before editing

Do not edit or publish while review sources are collecting findings. Wait for
local analysis to complete or become unavailable, refresh GitHub and Entire from
watcher events, and add every current item to the candidate queue.

When every available GitHub reviewer is `Current`, snapshot reviewer state,
unresolved/open sets, and newest timestamps, then start a 60-second quiet window.
Refresh at the end and for every watcher event. Reset the window only when an
authoritative state or timestamp changes; duplicate, reconnect, error, or
unfamiliar watcher events alone do not reset it.

A `Stale`, `Missing`, or `In flight` reviewer remains unsettled. An unavailable
source does not block useful work but prevents an unqualified clear result. Cap
collection at 15 minutes. At the cap, stop an unfinished local analysis and mark
it timed out, process the complete findings collected so far, leave unsettled
items open, and do not claim the queue is clear.

2. Treat unknown remote authors as human-owned.

Before editing, present every human, maintainer, and unknown-author item verbatim. For each item include its provider, location, author, stable ID, source-backed relevance assessment, current-code evidence, and the exact manual decision or in-person follow-up required.

Human feedback remains user-owned. Do not edit code, reply, resolve, dismiss, or otherwise publish an action for it unless the user explicitly selects that exact item after this presentation. Its unresolved status does not block independent automated work.

## 6. Classify automated feedback

For each automated item, re-read current source and its full remote context when
one exists, then assign exactly one of these actions:

- `Autofix eligible`: automated, source-backed, high confidence, minimal, unambiguous, in scope, and verifiable without a new dependency or a shared contract decision.

Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` only for a confirmed read-only query against local or development synthetic data. Never execute writes, migrations, production queries, or customer data for validation.
3. Record every command, exit status, and relevant output. If no code changed, skip code verification and state why.
4. When a required verification fails because of the fix, allow at most two focused repair rounds. If it still fails, report the failing command and output; do not commit, push, or publish code-fix statuses. Leave linked code-fix items open.
5. Do not call the result ready while required compile/build status is failing or unknown.

reuse the named `Hunk review` tab in the implementation workspace. Human Hunk
comments remain user-owned: address only the exact current comment set the user
selects after it is presented verbatim. If that review changes code, return to
section 8 and verify the final changed surface again before continuing.
When reporting the Herdr review surface, preserve the live `ID (name)`
references returned by `pfleidi:human-review`; do not replace them with bare
workspace, tab, or pane role phrases.

After the user approves the Hunk review, present one combined summary: grouped
issues, changed files, verification evidence, and the provider IDs awaiting
publication. Re-run the local `HEAD` and `headRefOid` alignment guard, then ask

Do not commit, push, reply to, resolve, or dismiss code-fix items without that approval and a successful push. 4. Keep human items, `Needs decision` items, ambiguous automated items, and unpushed code-fix items open. Return each successful update and exact failed operation/output.

# Create Pull Request

Use `origin/main` as the comparison base for understanding branch scope. Do not use local `main`, a local PR target branch, or direct tree diffs such as `git diff main` or `git diff origin/main` for scope checks; those can include upstream-only changes and make this branch look like it reverted unrelated work.

```bash

git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD
```

Review the changed file list from the merge base to the current working tree and confirm every changed file belongs to the PR's stated goal:

```bash
git diff --name-status <merge-base-sha>
```

If unrelated files or commits are present, STOP and report them. Do not create a PR that bundles unrelated work.

## 2. Sync with origin/main

Before discovering verification commands, bring the branch up to date with `origin/main` so verification runs against the merged state.

Check that the working tree is clean:

```bash
git status --short
```

If there are uncommitted changes, STOP and ask the user to commit or stash them before continuing. A sync into a dirty tree creates ambiguous failure states.

Fetch and merge:

```bash
git fetch origin main
git merge origin/main
```

Three outcomes:

- **Already up to date** — no commits to merge. Proceed to step 3.
- **Clean merge** — merge commit created (or fast-forward applied). Proceed to step 3.
- **Conflicts** — merge halts with conflicted files. Resolve safe conflicts
  autonomously using the rules below, complete the merge commit, then proceed
  to step 3. Do not stop merely because conflict markers exist.

### Resolve Merge Conflicts

When `git merge origin/main` conflicts, stay in the PR workflow and resolve the
merge unless a stop condition below applies. Completing the resulting merge
commit is part of the approved PR sync step; do not ask for separate commit
approval for that merge commit. This does not authorize unrelated commits,
amendments, rebases, resets, or force-pushes.

First inspect the conflict state:

```bash
git status --short
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U
git diff --cc
```

For each conflicted file:

1. Read the conflicted file and enough surrounding source to understand both
   sides.
2. Compare branch intent from step 1 with upstream changes from `origin/main`.
3. Keep both sides when they are independent additions.
4. Prefer the branch side only when upstream changed unrelated surrounding code
   and the branch behavior is still correct.
5. Prefer the upstream side only when the branch touched stale code that upstream
   replaced and the branch intent is still preserved elsewhere.
6. Edit the file so no conflict markers remain.
7. Re-check the file after editing.

Stop and ask the user only when a conflict requires judgment the agent cannot
source from the code or PR intent, such as:

- The two sides implement incompatible product or API behavior.
- A shared/public interface, schema, migration, generated file, lockfile, binary
  file, snapshot, or vendored file cannot be resolved confidently.
- Resolving would require broad refactoring outside the conflicted files.
- Either side deletes behavior the other side still appears to need.
- The conflict touches secrets, credentials, customer data, destructive
  operations, or deployment configuration in a way where the correct result is
  not obvious from source.

After resolving all conflicts:

```bash
git diff --check
git status --short
git add <resolved-files>
git commit --no-edit
```

Use the default merge commit message unless there is a clear reason to edit it.
Do not amend, reset, abort the merge, or force-push. If `git diff --check`
fails, fix the whitespace/conflict-marker issue before staging. If unresolved

1. **Makefile** — look for `build`, `lint`, `check`, `test`, `ci`, `verify` targets. Read the target recipes to understand what they run.
2. **mise** — check for `.mise.toml` or `.mise/*.toml`. Look for `[tasks]` definitions covering build, lint, test. If found, use `mise run <task>`.

4. **README.md** — look for "Development", "Contributing", "Building", or "Testing" sections that document how to run checks.
5. **Package manager conventions** — detect from project files:

   - `package.json` → check `scripts` for `build`, `lint`, `test`
   - `Cargo.toml` → `cargo build`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo test`

If no lint command exists after checking all sources, state that explicitly instead of assuming an unavailable linter binary.

### Reuse Cached Verification Discovery

The cache is only an input-token optimization; never commit it and never trust it blindly. If no artifact directory is available, perform normal discovery and skip writing the cache.

Reuse the cache only when all of these are true:

- It names the same worktree root and remote.
- It lists the verification source files it was based on, such as `Makefile`, `.mise.toml`, `.mise/*.toml`, CI workflow files, README files, and package manifests.
- Those source files still exist or are still intentionally absent.
- `git diff --name-only origin/main -- <source files>` shows no branch changes to those source files.

If the cache is missing, stale, or incomplete, perform normal discovery. After discovery, update the cache with:

- Repository root and remote.
- Verification source files inspected.
- Selected command plan grouped by coverage area.
- Commands intentionally skipped as duplicates, aggregate/subtask overlaps, CI-only jobs, or too-slow shard matrices.
- Any assumptions, such as "no documented lint task found."

### Deduplicate Verification Commands

Build a command plan by coverage area, not by source. Do not run every command discovered.

- Run at most one command for each coverage area: build/compile, lint/static analysis, unit/core tests, integration tests, e2e/smoke tests.
- Prefer documented local developer tasks over CI-specific commands when they cover the same area.
- Do not run both an aggregate task and its constituent tasks. For example, if `mise run check` runs lint and tests, either run `mise run check` alone or run the narrower lint/test tasks, not both.
- Treat CI matrix shards as duplicated slices of one suite. Do not run every `*:shard:*` command locally when an unsharded local task covers the suite.
- If CI has only sharded commands and no local equivalent, ask before running all shards. Otherwise, run the smallest representative or changed-scope test command and note that the full shard matrix remains for CI.
- Do not run CI-only canary/e2e jobs locally by default. Run them only when the PR changes that surface, when the user asks, or when the project documents them as required local PR verification.

Log which sources you used, which duplicate/CI-only commands you skipped, and what commands you will run. If the deduplication rules require asking before slow CI-only coverage, STOP for confirmation; otherwise immediately proceed to step 4.

## 4. Run Verification and Auto-Fix

Run the deduplicated command plan in the fewest safe batches. Prefer background processing for independent validation tasks instead of running everything sequentially.

The commands should cover, at minimum:
- **Build** — the project compiles without errors
- **Lint / static analysis** — no lint warnings or static analysis failures
- **Tests** — the selected local test coverage passes without duplicating CI shards or aggregate/subtask combinations

Use the exact commands, flags, and build tags found in step 3 for the commands you selected. Do not invent your own flags.

### Parallel Verification Rules

Partition the selected commands into dependency-safe batches before running them:

- Run mutating commands alone and before validators that depend on their output. This includes formatters, generators, codegen, migrations, package installation, or commands known to update snapshots, lockfiles, generated files, caches in the repo, or test fixtures.
- Run dependent commands after their prerequisite batch passes. For example, do not start tests that require generated code until generation succeeds.
- Run independent read-only validation commands concurrently in the same background batch. Build, lint/static analysis, typecheck/vet, and unit tests can usually share a batch when they do not mutate the working tree and do not require the same exclusive service, port, database, or fixture directory.
- Keep integration, e2e, or service-backed commands separate unless the project documents that they are parallel-safe.
- If unsure whether two commands are independent, run them sequentially. Correctness of validation beats speed.

For each background batch:

1. Start every command from the same working-tree state.
2. Run each selected validator directly, for example `mise run lint`, `go test ...`, or `npm test -- ...`. Do not wrap validators in `sh -c`, shell redirection, `tee`, command separators, or pipelines solely to capture logs; that defeats command-prefix approvals and causes extra permission prompts.
3. Capture each command's stdout, stderr, exit status, and command line from the tool output separately.
4. While the batch is running, do not edit files, start auto-fixes, or treat partial output as a result.
5. Wait for every command in the batch to finish, then show verification as a compact table:

   | Command | Exit | Relevant output |
   |---------|------|-----------------|
   | `go test ./pkg/foo -run TestBar -count=1` | 0 | Short success excerpt. |

6. For failures or short outputs, show complete output in the relevant-output column or immediately below the table. For long successful outputs, show the relevant excerpt and state that the rest was truncated.
7. If any command in the batch fails, treat the whole batch as failed for the fix loop. Results from other commands in that stale batch may help diagnose, but they do not count as passing verification after files change.

### On Failure: Fix and Re-verify

If any command fails, do NOT stop. Instead:

1. Read the error output and identify every failure
2. Fix all issues — apply the minimal changes needed to make the failing command pass
3. Re-run the deduplicated verification plan from the top, using the same safe batching rules (not just the previously failing command — fixes can introduce new issues)
4. Show the updated verification table again, including complete failure output for any command that still fails

Repeat this cycle until all commands pass. Cap at **3 fix attempts**. If verification still fails after 3 rounds, STOP and present the remaining failures to the user with full failure output — do not keep looping.

## 5. Prompt for Commit

After all verification passes, check for uncommitted changes:

```bash

```

If there are uncommitted changes (from auto-fixes in step 4):

1. Show the diff of all uncommitted changes
2. Propose a semantically correct commit message using the subject-plus-context style from `AGENTS.md`. The message must describe the net fix (e.g., "fix lint warnings in config parser" not "fix issues found during PR prep").
3. If compile/build did not pass for code changes, say the work is not commit-ready and do not ask to commit until the gap is resolved or the user explicitly takes over.
4. **STOP and wait for user approval.** The user may edit the message, split the changes, or commit themselves.

If the user approves the commit, do not rerun the full verification suite before committing unless files changed after step 4. If another sanity check is needed, use the commit-time verification scope from `AGENTS.md`: lint tasks, a compile/build check for code changes, and tests directly related to the changed code only.

If there are no uncommitted changes, proceed directly to step 6.

## 6. Push the Branch

```bash

```

If the branch has no upstream yet, use `git push -u origin HEAD`.

After the push succeeds, record the exact review candidate:

Set the target base branch from the user-provided PR base, or `main` when the user did not provide one. Scope checks still use `origin/main`; the PR target base controls only the GitHub PR destination.

Use `main` as the PR base branch unless the user provided a different PR target base.

Determine the pushed source branch:

```bash
git branch --show-current
```

Record the output as `HEAD_BRANCH`. If it is empty, STOP and report that PR creation needs a named local branch.

Determine the GitHub repository slug from the origin remote before writing the PR body:

```bash
git remote get-url origin
```

Record the output as `REMOTE_URL`. Extract `GITHUB_REPO` as `<owner>/<repo>` from these origin URL forms:

- `git@github.com:<owner>/<repo>.git`
- `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git`
- `ssh://git@github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git`
- `entire://<mirror-host>/gh/<owner>/<repo>`

- **What changed** — a short, factual summary of the net change. One or two sentences; the diff is the source of truth.

- **Rendered Markdown** (for mostly Markdown PRs) — links to the changed Markdown files rendered on GitHub.

- A "Test plan" or "Verification" section listing the CLI commands run. Verification already happened in step 4; the transcript doesn't help the reviewer.
- A list of newly added tests. The diff already shows them; the list rots when tests are renamed or moved.
- A file-by-file changes summary. The diff already shows this too.

```bash
  -f body="<body>" \
  -f head="{head-branch}" \
  -f base="{base-branch}" \

```
